parts.latex:
Show that the equation of the tangent to $y=c\ln x$ at $x=p$, where $p>0$, is

$$y=\dfrac{c}{p}x-c+c\ln p.$$
Find the value of $c$ such that the tangent from part (a) has a gradient of 1 and passes through the origin.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= c\ln x \\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{c}{x} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient of the tangent at $x = p$ is $\dfrac{c}{p}$.

At $x = p$, $y = c\ln p$.
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ y - c\ln p &= \dfrac{c}{p}(x - p) \\ y - c\ln p &= \dfrac{c}{p}x - c \\ y &= \dfrac{c}{p}x - c + c\ln p \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the tangent at $x = p$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{c}{p} = 1 \quad (\text{since the tangent has a gradient of } 1)$$
$$\therefore\ c = p$$
$$-c + c\ln p = 0 \quad (\text{since the tangent passes through the origin})$$
$$\begin{aligned} -c + c\ln c &= 0 \\ c(-1 + \ln c) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$c = 0 \text{ or } \ln c = 1$$
$$\therefore\ c = e \quad (\text{as } c > 0)$$
criteria: States that $\dfrac{c}{p} = 1$ or $-c + c\ln p = 0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The tangent passes through the origin and the point $(a, \cos a)$, so
$$m = \dfrac{\cos a}{a}$$
From the diagram $\cos a < 1$, so $m < \dfrac{1}{a}$.

At $x = 2\pi$ the curve has $\cos 2\pi = 1$. The tangent touches the curve where it is concave down, so near the peak at $2\pi$ the line lies above the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} m(2\pi) &> 1 \\ m &> \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{1}{2\pi} < m < \dfrac{1}{a}$$

$$f(x)=e^{-x}\sin x$$

parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $y=f(x)$. You do NOT need to check the nature of the stationary points.
Without using any further calculus, sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$, showing stationary points, any intercepts and asymptotes.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{-x^2}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-2xe^{-x^2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= x\left(-2xe^{-x^2}\right) + e^{-x^2} \\ &= (1-2x^2)e^{-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x) = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} (1-2x^2)e^{-x^2} &= 0 \\ 1 - 2x^2 &= 0 \\ x^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ x &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \text{ or } x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
When $x = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$f\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}e^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}$$
When $x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$f\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)e^{-\frac{1}{2}} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}$$
$\therefore$ The stationary points are
$$\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}\right)$$
and
$$\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2e}}\right)$$

parts.latex: Let the equation of a curve be $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{e^x+1}$. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at the point where $x=1$ in general form.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{(e^x+1)-e^xx}{(e^x+1)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^x(1-x)+1}{(e^x+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f'(1)=\dfrac{1}{(e+1)^2}$$
$$m_{\text{normal}}=-(e+1)^2$$
$$f(1)=\dfrac{1}{e+1}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y-\dfrac{1}{e+1} &= -(e+1)^2(x-1) \\ (e+1)y-1 &= -(e+1)^3x+(e+1)^3 \\ (e+1)^3x+(e+1)y-(1+(e+1)^3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using $y=mx+c$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{e+1} &= -(e+1)^2(1)+c \\ c &= \dfrac{1}{e+1}+(e+1)^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=-(e+1)^2x+\dfrac{1}{e+1}+(e+1)^2$$
$$\therefore\ (e+1)^3x+(e+1)y-1-(e+1)^3=0$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}f\left(e^x\right)=e^x f'\left(e^x\right)$$
Since $e^x>0$, this is zero only when $f'\left(e^x\right)=0$, that is, when $e^x$ equals the $x$-coordinate of a stationary point of $f$.

$e^x$ takes only positive values.

Of the three stationary points of $f$, two have positive $x$-coordinates (near $x=1$ and $x=2$) and one has a negative $x$-coordinate.

So $y=f\left(e^x\right)$ has 2 stationary points.

solutions.latex:
The gradients of $y=e\ln x$ and $y=ax^2+c$ at point of intersection are both equal to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(e\ln x) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{e}{x} &= 1 \\ x &= e \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ y=e$, so $y=ax^2+c$ has gradient of 1 at point $(e,e)$.
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[ax^2+c\right]=2ax$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2ax &= 1 \quad\text{at } x=e \\ 2a\cdot e &= 1 \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{2e} \end{aligned}$$
and $y=ax^2+c=e$ at $x=e$:
$$\begin{aligned} e &= \dfrac{1}{2e}\cdot e^2+c \\ e &= \dfrac{e}{2}+c \\ c &= \dfrac{e}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{1}{2e},\ c=\dfrac{e}{2}$$
criteria: Finds value of $a$, or equivalent merit

559.stem:
Let

$$g(x)=\int_{x^3}^{1}\sqrt{\tan(t)}\,dt$$

and let $F(t)$ be an antiderivative of $\sqrt{\tan(t)}$, where $0\le x\le 1$. (Do NOT try to find $F(t)$.)

parts.latex: Find an expression for $g(x)$ in terms of $F$.

Definite integrals.evidence: F(1) is a constant and F'(t)=√tan t
Definite integrals.reason: Must read g(x)=F(1)−F(x³) from the definite integral before differentiating; owner: diff question containing int gates on int.

solutions.latex:
$F$ is an antiderivative of $\sqrt{\tan t}$, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus, $\displaystyle\int_a^b\sqrt{\tan t}\,dt=F(b)-F(a)$:
$$g(x)=F(1)-F(x^3)$$

meta.check: FTC with upper limit 1, lower limit x^3.

solutions.latex:
$F(1)$ is a constant and $F'(t)=\sqrt{\tan t}$. Using the chain rule on $F(x^3)$:
$$\begin{aligned} g'(x)&=0-F'(x^3)\times3x^2\\ &=-3x^2\sqrt{\tan(x^3)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates $F(x^3)$ using the chain rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the gradient of the normal to the curve $y=\dfrac{x}{\tan x}$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\tan x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\sec^2 x\end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\tan x-x\sec^2 x}{\tan^2 x}$$
When $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned}m_T&=\dfrac{\tan\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{4}\sec^2\frac{\pi}{4}}{\tan^2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\\&=\dfrac{1-\frac{\pi}{4}\times 2}{1}\\&=1-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_N=-\dfrac{1}{m_T}$:
$$\begin{aligned}m_N&=\dfrac{-1}{1-\frac{\pi}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{2}{\pi-2}\\&=1.751938394\ldots\\&\approx 1.752\ (3\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly applies the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\sin 3x}\right)=e^{x\sin 3x}\times\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)$$
To find $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)$, use the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\sin 3x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=3\cos 3x \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\sin 3x)=\sin 3x\,(1)+x\cdot 3\cos 3x$$
Hence
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x\sin 3x}\right)=e^{x\sin 3x}\times(\sin 3x+3x\cos 3x)$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit
Determines the derivatives of $u$ and $v$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Show that the equation of the tangent is

$$y=x\sec^2 c-c\sec^2 c+\tan c$$
Show that the gradient of this tangent can be simplified to $\dfrac{c^2+1}{c^2}$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate, using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2 x$:
$$y'=\sec^2 x$$
When $x=c$: $y=\tan c$ and $y'=\sec^2 c$.

Equation of the tangent, using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-\tan c&=\sec^2 c\,(x-c)\\ y&=x\sec^2 c-c\sec^2 c+\tan c \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $y=\tan c$ and the gradient $\sec^2 c$, or equivalent merit
Finds $y=\tan c$ or $y'=\sec^2 c$ at $x=c$, or equivalent merit

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten marking guidelines (scanned pages, no text layer)

solutions.latex:
The tangent passes through $(0,-c)$; use $\sec^2 c=1+\tan^2 c$:
$$\begin{aligned} -c&=-c\sec^2 c+\tan c\\ -c&=-c(1+\tan^2 c)+\tan c\\ -c&=-c-c\tan^2 c+\tan c\\ c\tan^2 c-\tan c&=0\\ \tan c\,(c\tan c-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$\tan c=0$ gives $c=0$, not possible since $c\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. So $\tan c=\dfrac{1}{c}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan^2 c&=\dfrac{1}{c^2}\\ 1+\tan^2 c&=\dfrac{1}{c^2}+1\\ \sec^2 c&=\dfrac{1+c^2}{c^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{gradient}=\dfrac{c^2+1}{c^2}$$
Alternative: from $\tan c=\dfrac{1}{c}$ and the points $(0,-c)$, $(c,\tan c)$,
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{\tan c+c}{c-0}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{c}+c}{c}\\ &=\dfrac{1+c^2}{c}\times\dfrac{1}{c}\\ &=\dfrac{1+c^2}{c^2} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The line $y=mx$ is a tangent to the curve $y=\ln(kx)$, where $k>0$.

Find the value of $m$, in terms of $k$.

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at the point of contact:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln(kx)\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{k}{kx}=\dfrac{1}{x}\\ m&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
At the point of contact the line and the curve meet:
$$mx=\ln(kx)$$
Substituting $m=\dfrac{1}{x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\ln(kx)&=\dfrac{1}{x}\times x\\ \ln(kx)&=1\\ kx&=e\\ x&=\dfrac{e}{k}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore m=\dfrac{1}{\frac{e}{k}}=\dfrac{k}{e}$$
criteria: Finds $x$ in terms of $k$, or equivalent merit
Finds $m$ in terms of $x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=\dfrac{\ln(x-1)}{x-1}$ at the point $(2,0)$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln(x-1) & v&=x-1\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x-1} & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{\frac{1}{x-1}\times(x-1)-\ln(x-1)}{(x-1)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{1-\ln(x-1)}{(x-1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
At $x=2$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\dfrac{1-\ln(2-1)}{(2-1)^2}=1$$
Hence the gradient of the normal is $-1$ (negative reciprocal).

Using the point-gradient formula for the normal through $(2,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-0&=-1(x-2)\\ \therefore\ y&=2-x \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the equation of the tangent instead of the normal, or finds the gradient of the normal but not the equation of the normal, or equivalent merit
Correctly applies quotient rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the exact equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\log_2 x$ at the point where $x=4$.

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_a x=\dfrac{1}{x\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\dfrac{1}{(\ln 2)x}\\ m_T&=\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2} &&(x=4) \end{aligned}$$
At $x=4$, $y=\log_2 4=2$.

Using the point-gradient formula:
$$\begin{aligned} y-y_1&=m(x-x_1)\\ y-2&=\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2}(x-4)\\ y&=\dfrac{x}{4\ln 2}-\dfrac{1}{\ln 2}+2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds correct $y'$ AND either correct gradient or $y$ value, or equivalent merit
Finds correct $y'$ OR correct $y$ value, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Hence show that $y=x^2e^{x^2}$ is decreasing for all $x<0$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{x^2}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=2xe^{x^2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2e^{x^2}\right)&=e^{x^2}\times 2x+x^2\times 2xe^{x^2}\\ &=2xe^{x^2}+2x^3e^{x^2}\\ &=2xe^{x^2}\left(1+x^2\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to use the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $y'=2xe^{x^2}\left(1+x^2\right)$. When $x<0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2x&<0\\ e^{x^2}&>0\\ 1+x^2&>0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=\text{negative}\times\text{positive}\times\text{positive}\\ &=\text{negative} \end{aligned}$$
Hence $y$ is decreasing for all $x<0$.

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=e^x+\log_e(4x-3)$ at the point where $x=1$.

solutions.latex:
$$y=e^x+\ln(4x-3)$$
Differentiating, with the chain rule for $\ln(4x-3)$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^x+\dfrac{1}{4x-3}\times4$$
When $x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e+\ln(4-3)\\&=e\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=e+\dfrac{4}{4-3}\\&=e+4\end{aligned}$$
The tangent passes through $(1,e)$ with gradient $m=e+4$. Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-e&=(e+4)(x-1)\\y&=(e+4)x-e-4+e\\&=(e+4)x-4\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the point $(1,e)$ or the gradient $e+4$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Determine the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\ln\left(3x^2+2\right)$ at the point $(2,\ \ln 14)$. Express your answer in general form $ax+by+c=0$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln\left(3x^2+2\right)\\ y'&=\dfrac{6x}{3x^2+2}\end{aligned}$$
At $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{6(2)}{3(2)^2+2}\\ &=\dfrac{6}{7}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ m=\dfrac{6}{7}$ at $(2,\ln 14)$.

Using the point-gradient form $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-\ln 14&=\dfrac{6}{7}(x-2)\\ 7y-7\ln 14&=6x-12\\ 6x-7y+7\ln 14-12&=0\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient $\dfrac{6}{7}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following is the derivative of $e^{3^x x^6}$.

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} u&=3^x & v&=x^6 \\ u'&=3^x\log_e3 & v'&=6x^5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(3^xx^6\right)=3^x\log_e3\cdot x^6+6x^5\cdot3^x=3^xx^5\left(6+x\log_e3\right)$$
By the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{g(x)}=g'(x)e^{g(x)}$:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{3^xx^6}=3^xx^5\left(6+x\log_e3\right)e^{3^xx^6}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{\ln x}\right) &= \dfrac{3x^2\ln x-x^3\cdot\frac{1}{x}}{(\ln x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{3x^2\ln x-x^2}{(\ln x)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the quotient rule with $u$, $v$, $u'$ and $v'$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the equation of the normal to the curve $y=e^{\cos(\pi x)}$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{u}\right)=u'e^{u}$ with $u=\cos\pi x$:
$$y'=-\pi\sin\pi x\cdot e^{\cos\pi x}$$
At $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$, the gradient of the tangent is
$$\begin{aligned} m_T &= -\pi\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot e^{\cos\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= -\pi(1)e^0 \\ &= -\pi \end{aligned}$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent:
$$\begin{aligned} m_N &= -\dfrac{1}{m_T} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
When $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $y=e^{\cos\frac{\pi}{2}}=e^0=1$, so the point is $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},1\right)$. The normal is
$$\begin{aligned} y-1 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi}\left(x-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ \pi y-\pi &= x-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ 2x-2\pi y+2\pi-1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Equivalently, $y=\dfrac{1}{\pi}x-\dfrac{1}{2\pi}+1$.
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Hence show that if $y=\log_x 2$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{\ln 2}{x(\ln x)^2}$

solutions.latex:
Use the change of base rule, $\log_ab=\dfrac{\log_cb}{\log_ca}$, with base $2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\log_x2\\ &=\dfrac{\log_22}{\log_2x}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\log_2x}\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Shows change of base formula (essential step)
meta.marker_note: The change of base step is essential and must be shown.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $y=\log_x2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2x}$. Change the base to $e$ using $\log_2x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{\ln x}{\ln2}}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln2}{\ln x}\\ &=\ln2\cdot(\ln x)^{-1}\end{aligned}$$
Differentiate using the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\ln2\cdot(-1)(\ln x)^{-2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{x}\\ &=-\dfrac{\ln2}{x(\ln x)^2}\end{aligned}$$
